id: To J.G. On the News of His Marriage

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My Love? alas! I must not call you Mine, But to your envy’d Bride that Name resign: I must forget your lovely melting Charms, And be for ever Banisht from your Arms: For ever? oh! the Horror of that Sound! It gives my bleeding Heart a deadly wound: While I might hope, although my Hope was vain, It gave some Ease to my unpitty’d Pain, But now your Hymen doth all Hope exclude, And but to think is Sin; yet you intrude On every Thought; if I but close my Eyes, Methinks your pleasing Form besides me lies; With every Sigh I gently breath your Name, Yet no ill Thoughts pollute my hallow’d Flame; ’Tis pure and harmless, as a Lambent Fire, And never mingled with a warm Desire: All I have now to ask of Bounteous Heaven, Is, that your Perjuries may be forgiven: That she who you have with your Nuptials blest, As She’s the Happiest Wife, may prove the Best: That all our Joys may light on you alone, Then I can be contented to have none: And never wish that you shou’d kinder be, Than now and then, to cast a Thought on Me: And, Madam, though the Conquest you have won, Over my Strephon, has my hopes undone; I’le daily beg of Heaven, he may be Kinder to You, than he has been to Me.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Love, Mine, But

outputs.L1:
My love? Alas, I must not call you mine,  
But to your envied bride that name resign.  
I must forget your lovely, melting charms,  
And be forever banished from your arms.  

Forever? Oh, the horror of that sound!  
It gives my bleeding heart a deadly wound.  
While I could hope—although that hope was vain—  
It brought some solace to my unpitied pain.  

But now your marriage must all hope exclude,  
And even thought is sin; yet you intrude  
On every thought. If I but close my eyes,  
I seem to see your pleasing form beside me lie.  

With every sigh, I gently breathe your name,  
Yet no impure thought stains my hallowed flame.  
’Tis pure and harmless as a lambent fire,  
And never mingled with a warmer desire.  

All I have now to ask of bounteous Heaven  
Is that your perjuries may be forgiven;  
That she whom you have with your nuptials blessed,  
As she’s the happiest wife, may prove the best;  

That all our joys may light on you alone—  
Then I can be content to possess none—  
And never wish that you should kinder be  
Than now and then to cast a thought on me.  

And, Madam, though the conquest you have won  
Over my Strephon has my hopes undone,  
I’ll daily beg of Heaven that he may be  
Kinder to you than he has been to me.
outputs.L2:
My beloved—no, I no longer have the right to claim you;  
That title now belongs to your fortunate bride.  
I must erase the memory of your tender beauty  
And accept that I am forever barred from your embrace.  
Forever! The very word fills me with terror  
And strikes a fatal blow against my wounded heart.  

Even when I knew my hopes could never be fulfilled,  
Their presence brought a little comfort to my neglected grief.  
But your marriage has now extinguished every possibility,  
And even imagining otherwise has become sinful.  
Still, you enter every thought I have.  
Whenever I shut my eyes, I seem to see  
Your beloved figure resting close beside me.  
Each quiet breath and sigh carries your name,  
Though no impure idea stains my sacred affection.  
My love is innocent and gentle, like a soft, flickering flame,  
Never joined with physical longing.  

Only this remains for me to request from generous Heaven:  
May you be pardoned for the vows you broke,  
And may the woman blessed by becoming your wife—  
Already the happiest of wives—also prove the finest.  
May every joy that might have been ours fall to you alone;  
If you are happy, I can endure having no happiness myself.  
I ask for no greater kindness from you  
Than that you occasionally remember me.  

And, Madam, although your triumph in winning my Strephon  
Has destroyed every hope I once possessed,  
I will pray each day that Heaven ensures  
He treats you more kindly than he ever treated me.
outputs.L3:
The speaker mourns the marriage of her beloved to another woman, recognizing that he is now forever beyond her reach. His marriage extinguishes the last of her hope and intensifies the sorrow of their separation, yet she remains unable to forget him. He continues to occupy her thoughts, even though any possibility of their being together has disappeared.

At the same time, she insists that her love is pure, untouched by sinful or physical desire. Although he has broken his promises and caused her profound pain, she does not respond with bitterness or revenge. Instead, she prays that he will be forgiven and hopes that his bride will prove to be a worthy, loving, and happy wife.

Ultimately, the speaker places the couple’s happiness above her own grief. She sincerely wishes them joy in their marriage, asking only that her former beloved remember her from time to time. Her final hope is that he will treat his wife with greater kindness and faithfulness than he once showed her.
outputs.L4:
The poem takes the form of a deeply personal lament spoken in the first person. Addressing the man she loves directly, the speaker confronts the painful reality that he has married another woman and is therefore lost to her. Her words reveal the intimacy of their former bond, but they also mark a deliberate act of renunciation. Although she cannot immediately extinguish her feelings, she recognizes that she must give up every hope of sharing a future with him.

This renunciation, however, is neither simple nor emotionally complete. The speaker continues to love him with an intensity that marriage and separation cannot erase. Her attachment remains persistent but chaste: she does not seek to interfere with his new relationship, nor does she demand that he return to her. Instead, she struggles privately against memory, longing, and grief. The direct address makes this conflict especially immediate, as though she is speaking both to her beloved and to herself, trying to accept what her heart still resists.

The poem’s emotional force lies in the contrast between inward suffering and outward restraint. The speaker’s sorrow is profound, yet she refuses to turn it into bitterness or accusation. She acknowledges the other woman’s rightful place and attempts to withdraw with dignity. In doing so, she transforms romantic loss into a test of moral strength. Her love is shown to be genuine precisely because it does not become possessive: even when she cannot have the man she loves, she does not wish to destroy his happiness.

By the end of the poem, grief develops into selfless goodwill. The speaker prays for the happiness of the married couple, placing their peace above her own desires. This blessing does not erase her pain; rather, it makes her sacrifice more moving. Her acceptance is painful because her love remains alive, yet it is dignified because she chooses generosity over resentment. The poem therefore presents renunciation not as emotional indifference, but as the highest and most difficult expression of devotion. Through her willingness to suffer silently and wish happiness upon others, the speaker reveals both the depth of her love and the courage required to let it go.
outputs.L5:
Love was never mine to keep, but it was mine to feel.  
For a moment, your hand fit perfectly in mine, and the world seemed quiet enough for forever. But forever is a promise life does not always honor.

Still, I do not regret loving you. Some people stay in our lives; others remain only in our hearts. You may no longer be mine, but the love we shared will always be part of me.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Restoration-era poem in the voice of a woman lamenting that her beloved Strephon has married another, while generously wishing happiness upon his bride.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Forsaken Nymph’s Good Wish**

When first the cruel tidings reach’d mine ear,  
I chid the tongue that taught my heart to fear;  
Yet Fame, too faithful in my grief alone,  
Proclaim’d my Strephon was another’s own.  

No more beneath the myrtle’s secret shade  
His vows shall charm the fond, believing maid;  
Those eyes, whose light my willing soul betray’d,  
Now bless the fairer choice that Love has made.  

Yet, Heav’n, forbid my sorrow should destroy  
One tender moment of her bridal joy:  
May she possess him constant, kind, and true,  
Nor ever mourn what I too surely knew.  

May every grace attend her happy reign,  
And Hymen bind with flowers his golden chain;  
May no cold doubt her gentle breast molest,  
But Strephon’s image sleep within it blest.  

For me, I’ll teach my tears in shades to flow,  
Where none shall triumph, and where none shall know;  
Content, though exil’d from the joys I prize,  
To wish her happy—while her rival dies.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rhyming farewell letter in archaic English from an abandoned lover to a newly married man and his wife.
counterfactuals.output:
**To My Once-Belovèd, and His New-Wedded Bride**

Good sir, and thou, his lady fair,  
Give ear unto my last despair;  
Though once his vows were sworn to me,  
I yield him now, fair wife, to thee.  

He called mine eyes his morning star,  
Yet sought a brighter light afar;  
His faith, once writ in words of gold,  
Like winter’s breath hath vanished cold.  

Yet blame I not thy gentle hand,  
Nor thee who wear’st his wedding-band;  
Perchance thou knew’st not how his vow  
Had bound another heart ere now.  

And thou, false love, whom once I blessed,  
Go lay thy head upon her breast;  
Mayhap the truth thou couldst not keep  
Shall trouble not her quiet sleep.  

I shall not haunt thy bridal door,  
Nor plead, nor curse, nor chide thee more;  
My tears shall fall where none may see,  
And time unteach thy name to me.  

So fare ye well, both bride and groom;  
May roses guard your gilded room.  
Though mine own rose lie crushed and dead,  
No thorn shall crown thy marriage-bed.  

Take thou the ring I ne’er did wear,  
Take back each oath dissolved in air;  
I loose thee from my heart’s last claim—  
God grant I soon forget thy name.  

Thus ends the love thou didst forsake;  
Thus dawns the path that I must take.  
Farewell, false heart; farewell, fair wife—  
I leave ye both, and choose my life.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a 17th-century-style lyric about unrequited love, lost hope, pure devotion, forgiveness, and self-sacrifice.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Votive Song**

When first thy star rose in mine eyes,  
I deem’d no night could be;  
Yet now beneath forsaken skies  
I keep my watch for thee.  

My hope, once green as April’s bough,  
Lies pale beneath the snow;  
Still at thy silent shrine I bow,  
Though thou wilt never know.  

No thorn thy gentle hand hath set  
Shall move my heart to blame;  
I pardon all, and love thee yet,  
As tapers guard a flame.  

Take thou the morn, the rose, the May,  
The music and the mirth;  
I’ll bear the darkness of thy way,  
And ask no heaven on earth.  

If grief may purchase thee one breath  
Untroubled, glad, and free,  
Then welcome sorrow, exile, death—  
So peace abide with thee.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dramatic poetic monologue beginning “My Love? alas! I must not call you Mine,” in which the speaker renounces her beloved after his wedding.
counterfactuals.output:
“My Love? alas! I must not call you Mine,”  
The bells have sealed what silence could not sever;  
Another hand is folded now in thine,  
Another bears thy name—and bears it ever.  

I watched the white doors open like a wound,  
And heard the organ thunder out my doom;  
While blessings fell, and smiling faces crowned  
Your vows, I stood unseen amid the gloom.  

No tear betrayed me. Proudly I endured  
To see her veil brush softly at thy side;  
To hear the sacred promise that assured  
The world she was—and I was not—thy bride.  

Yet once, beneath the summer’s trembling star,  
You called me heart, and hope, and heaven above.  
How near those vanished midnight gardens are!  
How far the morning carries us from love!  

Keep, then, the ring your chosen hand has taken;  
Keep every vow the altar heard you say.  
I will not haunt the happiness you’ve wakened,  
Nor cast my shadow darkly on her day.  

But if, when winter presses at the pane,  
A half-remembered voice should trouble thee—  
If some old song should breathe my name again,  
Oh, turn not from her gentle face to me.  

For I renounce thee—not because love dies,  
But that it lives too deeply to betray.  
I close my heart as twilight closes skies,  
And bless the star that must not bid me stay.  

Go—be her joy. Let all my dreams depart;  
I give thee up, though giving rends the giver.  
Thou art no longer mine before the world—  
But lost within my soul, thou livest ever.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an imitation of an early modern English complaint poem addressed first to a faithless lover and then to the woman who has won him, using elevated diction, heroic couplets, and names such as Strephon.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Forsaken Nymph’s Complaint**

O Strephon, once the glory of my plain,  
Why dost thou make my faithful bosom vain?  
Those vows which trembling at my feet were made  
Now, like faint stars before the morn, do fade.  

Thou call’dst my eyes twin lamps of heavenly fire,  
My voice the sacred music of thy lyre;  
Yet now those eyes in fruitless torrents flow,  
That voice is tuned to elegies of woe.  

Was it for this I crown’d thy brow with bays,  
And fed thy pride with never-ceasing praise?  
Was it for this, beneath the myrtle grove,  
I gave thee all my innocence and love?  

False shepherd, go; pursue thy new delight,  
And court her shadow through the faithless night.  
Yet when her beauty, like the rose, is fled,  
Remember her whose heart thy change hath bled.  

But thou, fair Chloris, victor of my swain,  
Triumph not proudly in another’s pain.  
The prize thou wear’st was purchasèd by my tears;  
Thy present joy is built upon my fears.  

Believe not all his sighs, though sweet they prove,  
Nor take his perjuries for seals of love.  
The tongue that now thy matchless grace doth raise  
Once made my humbler charms its only praise.  

To thee he swears the sun itself is dim;  
He swore the selfsame flattering oath to me.  
To thee his heart he offers, whole and free—  
A broken gift, long forfeited by thee.  

Enjoy him, then, till some more radiant face  
Shall from thy brow the borrowed garland chase.  
For Strephon’s faith, like April skies, is clear  
Only to darken ere the noon appear.  

And when, forsaken, thou shalt weep alone,  
Thy grief shall teach thee how to pity mine;  
Then shall we join, by equal sorrow led,  
To mourn one living man as doubly dead.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
